Ranking Each Variable on Its Significance

library(broom)
library(dplyr)

# Remove Age from predictor list
predictors <- setdiff(names(abalone), "Age")

results <- lapply(predictors, function(var) {

  # Build formula dynamically
  formula <- as.formula(paste("Age ~", var))
  model <- lm(formula, data = abalone)

  # If variable is numeric → use coefficient p-value
  if (is.numeric(abalone[[var]])) {
    tidy_res <- tidy(model)[2, ]  # predictor row
    p_val <- tidy_res$p.value
    estimate <- tidy_res$estimate
    t_val <- tidy_res$statistic
  } else {
    # categorical → use ANOVA model-level p-value
    p_val <- glance(model)$p.value
    estimate <- NA
    t_val <- NA
  }

  data.frame(
    Variable = var,
    Estimate = estimate,
    t_value = t_val,
    p_value = p_val,
    R_squared = summary(model)$r.squared,
    Type = ifelse(is.numeric(abalone[[var]]), "Numeric", "Categorical")
  )
})

results_df <- bind_rows(results)

# Sort by statistical significance (smallest p-value first)
best_predictors <- results_df %>%
  arrange(p_value)

best_predictors
##             Variable     Estimate    t_value   p_value    R_squared        Type
## value            Sex           NA         NA 0.0000000 0.2962139965 Categorical
## ...2        Diameter 8.593726e+00  99.155518 0.0000000 0.3959681559     Numeric
## ...3          Length 7.010585e+00  97.146658 0.0000000 0.3862201907     Numeric
## ...4          Height 2.372570e+01 109.025933 0.0000000 0.4421352796     Numeric
## ...5          Weight 1.574955e-01  95.270225 0.0000000 0.3770149967     Numeric
## ...6  Shucked.Weight 2.907932e-01  71.462260 0.0000000 0.2540110189     Numeric
## ...7  Viscera.Weight 6.785554e-01  87.875999 0.0000000 0.3398823163     Numeric
## ...8    Shell.Weight 6.239705e-01 115.349319 0.0000000 0.4701002214     Numeric
## ...9              id 1.004409e-05   1.633207 0.1024465 0.0001778164     Numeric

All predictors individually show significance to predicting Age with the Sex categorical being the highest one with the lowest p-value. We will keep sex in our final model as an interaction term not one because it is our only categorical variable and may help make better predictions but also because it is overwhelmingly significant. We will look more into these numeric predictors to make sure they satisfy the assumptions of the linear model and check for any influential observations.

Renaming Variable to get rid of spaces for better reference of the variables:

abalone <- abalone %>%
  rename(
    Viscera_Weight = `Viscera.Weight`,
    Shell_Weight   = `Shell.Weight`,
    Shucked_Weight = `Shucked.Weight`
  )

Initial Matrix Scatter Plot of the Data

ggpairs(
  abalone,
  columns = c(
    "Age", "Diameter", "Length", "Height",
    "Weight", "Shucked_Weight", "Viscera_Weight", "Shell_Weight"
  )
)

There visually looks to be a positive correlation between each predictor variable and the target response. There are some noticeable predictors that are correlated with each other which is important to keep in mind when considering co-linearity in developing our predictive model to which these co- linear predictor variables could be telling us the same story and inflating the variance of our model. Predictors that stand out to causing this are the Weights and subsets of Weight (Viscera, Shell, and Shucked Weights) as well as of the size variables Diameter x Length, Diameter x Height, and Height x Length.

First Step is to Check the Assumptions of the Full Model

# Encode Sex as factor
abalone$Sex <- factor(abalone$Sex, levels = c("I", "M", "F"))

# Full model
full_mod <- lm(Age ~ Sex + Length + Diameter + Height +
                 Weight + Shucked_Weight + Viscera_Weight + Shell_Weight,
               data = abalone)
summary(full_mod)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Age ~ Sex + Length + Diameter + Height + Weight +

## Height          9.75327    0.59612  16.361   <2e-16 ***
## Weight          0.21717    0.01193  18.201   <2e-16 ***

As an initial baseline model, having all the predictors in the model with a low adjusted R^2 and Length and Height are no significant to effecting Age. Because of this we will dive deeper to check for those co linear variables that could be causing our model to over fit, check for any influential observations we may remove and of course check for the assumptions on a linear regression model.

Checking Assumptions for Full Model

# Linearity
# Partial residual plots for all predictors
crPlots(full_mod)

From the partial Residual Plots, there seems to be some variables with impact on Age indicating they might be confusing our model by telling it the same thing. Length and Diameter combined aren’t saying much about age given the straight line in both.

# Normaility
# Q-Q plot
qqPlot(full_mod, main = "Q-Q Plot of Residuals")

## [1] 8952 9845
# Histogram
hist(residuals(full_mod), breaks = 40, main = "Residual Histogram")

# Equal Variance 
# Global Diagnostic Plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(full_mod)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

From the residual scatter plot and Q-Q plot there seems to be evidence against equal variation with some influential points.

Checking for Influential Points and Co-linear Predictors

# Check Multi-collinearity (VIF)
vif(full_mod)
##                     GVIF Df GVIF^(1/(2*Df))
## Sex             1.959899  2        1.183201
## Length         64.042730  1        8.002670
## Diameter       67.683069  1        8.226972
## Height         10.339787  1        3.215554
## Weight         80.163585  1        8.953412
## Shucked_Weight 22.195874  1        4.711250
## Viscera_Weight 19.941965  1        4.465643
## Shell_Weight   22.641391  1        4.758297

To assess multicollinearity in the initial full model, we examined the generalized variance inflation factors (GVIFs) for all predictors. The categorical variable Sex showed a very low adjusted GVIF of 1.18, indicating no collinearity concerns. In contrast, the core size and mass variables Length, Diameter, and Weight exhibited substantially elevated GVIF values (approximately 8.0, 8.2, and 9.0, respectively), signaling serious multicollinearity among these predictors. The component weight measures—Shucked Weight, Viscera Weight, and Shell Weight—also showed moderately high GVIFs in the range of 4.5 to 4.8, suggesting that they share considerable information with overall Weight and with each other. Collectively, these results indicate that the full model includes a cluster of highly correlated size and weight variables, which inflates standard errors and undermines the stability and interpretability of individual coefficient estimates. This motivated a targeted reduction of redundant predictors in the next modeling step, while retaining a smaller set of biologically meaningful size and mass variables.

Fit Reduced Model After Eliminating Predictors with High Variance Inflation

reduced_mod <- lm(Age ~ Sex + Length + Height + Weight + Shell_Weight,
                  data = abalone)
summary(reduced_mod)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Age ~ Sex + Length + Height + Weight + Shell_Weight, 
##     data = abalone)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max

## (Intercept)   3.878764   0.157741  24.590   <2e-16 ***

## SexF          1.152009   0.059874  19.241   <2e-16 ***
## Length       -0.263114   0.218035  -1.207    0.228    
## Height       11.373567   0.629192  18.076   <2e-16 ***

## F-statistic:  2910 on 6 and 14993 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
# Recheck VIF for Colinearity
vif(reduced_mod)
##                   GVIF Df GVIF^(1/(2*Df))
## Sex           1.938395  2        1.179942
## Length       12.122985  1        3.481808
## Height       10.090525  1        3.176559
## Weight       20.022006  1        4.474596
## Shell_Weight 17.621774  1        4.197830

Co-linearity Seems to be handled now. All VIF below 5 which is acceptable.

# Rechecking Linearity 
crPlots(reduced_mod)

After reducing the model to address multicollinearity, we re‑examined the linearity assumption using component-plus-residual plots. The plot for Length showed a clear linear trend, with the lowess smooth closely following the fitted line. The plots for Height, Weight, and Shell Weight displayed only mild upward curvature, but the deviations from linearity were small and not strongly suggestive of a misspecified functional form. Because the observed curvature was subtle, transformations were not strictly required; however, polynomial terms could be considered to improve predictive accuracy. To determine whether transformations meaningfully improved model performance, we compared the reduced model with and without squared terms using AIC, adjusted R², and RMSE.

# Normaility
# Q-Q plot
qqPlot(reduced_mod, main = "Q-Q Plot of Residuals")

## [1]  9845 10524
# Histogram
hist(residuals(reduced_mod), breaks = 40, main = "Residual Histogram")

# Equal Variance 
# Global Diagnostic Plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(reduced_mod)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Fitting the Reduced Transformed Model to Compare with Reduced

abalone$Height2 <- abalone$Height^2
abalone$Weight2 <- abalone$Weight^2
abalone$ShellWeight2 <- abalone$Shell_Weight^2
reduced_mod_transformed <- lm(
  Age ~ Sex + Length + Height + Height2 +
         Weight + Weight2 + Shell_Weight + ShellWeight2,
  data = abalone
)
summary(reduced_mod_transformed)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Age ~ Sex + Length + Height + Height2 + Weight + 
##     Weight2 + Shell_Weight + ShellWeight2, data = abalone)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -7.4278 -1.2935 -0.3319  0.7558 17.1717 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   3.982e+00  2.415e-01  16.488  < 2e-16 ***
## SexM          7.670e-01  5.798e-02  13.228  < 2e-16 ***
## SexF          9.423e-01  6.154e-02  15.313  < 2e-16 ***
## Length       -4.554e+00  3.417e-01 -13.326  < 2e-16 ***
## Height        2.939e+01  1.959e+00  15.005  < 2e-16 ***
## Height2      -2.886e+01  2.671e+00 -10.806  < 2e-16 ***
## Weight       -2.022e-01  1.945e-02 -10.397  < 2e-16 ***
## Weight2       4.012e-04  2.404e-04   1.669   0.0951 .  
## Shell_Weight  1.597e+00  6.368e-02  25.084  < 2e-16 ***
## ShellWeight2 -2.264e-02  2.851e-03  -7.939 2.18e-15 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 2.195 on 14990 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.5472, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5469 
## F-statistic:  2013 on 9 and 14990 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
# Code for Evaluating Reduced Model vs Reduced Model After Transformations
# Fit models
reduced_mod <- lm(Age ~ Sex + Length + Height + Weight + Shell_Weight,
                  data = abalone)

reduced_mod_transformed <- lm(Age ~ Sex + Length + Height + Height2 +
         Weight + Weight2 + Shell_Weight + ShellWeight2,
  data = abalone)

# AIC comparison
AIC(reduced_mod, reduced_mod_transformed)
##                         df      AIC
## reduced_mod              8 66468.02
## reduced_mod_transformed 11 66171.23
# Adjusted R²
print("Reduced Model R^2:") 
## [1] "Reduced Model R^2:"
summary(reduced_mod)$adj.r.squared
## [1] 0.5377981
print("Reduced Transformed Model R^2:") 
## [1] "Reduced Transformed Model R^2:"
summary(reduced_mod_transformed)$adj.r.squared
## [1] 0.5469441
# RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)
rmse_reduced <- rmse(abalone$Age, predict(reduced_mod))
rmse_reduced_transformed <- rmse(abalone$Age, predict(reduced_mod_transformed))

print("Reduced Model RSME:")
## [1] "Reduced Model RSME:"
rmse_reduced
## [1] 2.216942
print("Reduced Transformed Model RSME:") 
## [1] "Reduced Transformed Model RSME:"
rmse_reduced_transformed
## [1] 2.194679

To evaluate whether adding polynomial terms improved model performance, we compared the reduced linear model to the reduced transformed model using AIC, adjusted R², and RMSE. The transformed model achieved a noticeably lower AIC (66171.23 vs. 66468.02), indicating a better balance of fit and model complexity. It also produced a slightly higher adjusted R² (0.547 vs. 0.538), suggesting that the transformed predictors explained more variability in abalone age. Finally, the transformed model yielded a lower RMSE (2.195 vs. 2.217), reflecting modestly improved predictive accuracy. Taken together, these metrics show that incorporating the squared terms for Height, Weight, and Shell Weight resulted in a better‑fitting and more accurate model than the reduced linear specification.

Now Rechecking Assumptions on Reduced Transformed Model

# Rechecking Linearity 
crPlots(reduced_mod_transformed)

Linearity is Satified

# Normaility
# Q-Q plot
qqPlot(reduced_mod_transformed, main = "Q-Q Plot of Residuals")
## Warning in rlm.default(x, y, weights, method = method, wt.method = wt.method, :
## 'rlm' failed to converge in 20 steps

## [1] 8952 9845
# Histogram
hist(residuals(reduced_mod_transformed), breaks = 40, main = "Residual Histogram")

Normality looks fine with slight evidence of influential outlier from the upward bend on the Q-Q Plot and the slight right skewness of the resdidual histogram.

# Equal Variance 
# Global Diagnostic Plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(reduced_mod_transformed)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Equal Variance seems satisfied with randomly scatter residuals.

Now that we have a more stable model we will look into the influntial outliers.

# Checking for Influential Outliers
plot(reduced_mod_transformed, which = 4)  # Cook's distance

influencePlot(reduced_mod_transformed)

##         StudRes          Hat       CookD
## 523   -3.436332 0.1564200612 0.218797979
## 1821  -2.183634 0.0391698760 0.019433724
## 8952   7.796043 0.0009569982 0.005798918
## 9845   7.838528 0.0002854525 0.001747348
## 12004  3.878820 0.0157908358 0.024116270

To assess the influence of individual observations on the reduced transformed model, we examined Studentized residuals, leverage (hat values), and Cook’s Distance. Observation 523 emerged as a potential concern, with a large negative residual (−3.44), high leverage (0.156), and a Cook’s D of 0.219 — indicating that it has a disproportionate impact on the fitted model. Other observations, such as 8952 and 9845, exhibited extreme residuals but had very low leverage and Cook’s D values, suggesting they are not influential. Based on these diagnostics, only observation 523 warrants further investigation or sensitivity analysis to determine whether its removal meaningfully alters model estimates.

Refitting the Model without Observation 523 and Comparing Results

# Removing Observation 523 without changing original data
abalone_clean <- abalone[-523, ]

# Fit models
reduced_mod_transformed <- lm(Age ~ Sex + Length + Height + Height2 +
         Weight + Weight2 + Shell_Weight + ShellWeight2,
  data = abalone)

reduced_mod_transformed_clean <- lm(Age ~ Sex + Length + Height + Height2 +
         Weight + Weight2 + Shell_Weight + ShellWeight2,
  data = abalone_clean
)

# AIC comparison
AIC(reduced_mod_transformed, reduced_mod_transformed_clean)
## Warning in AIC.default(reduced_mod_transformed, reduced_mod_transformed_clean):
## models are not all fitted to the same number of observations
##                               df      AIC
## reduced_mod_transformed       11 66171.23
## reduced_mod_transformed_clean 11 66156.01
# Adjusted R²
print("Transformed Model R^2:")
## [1] "Transformed Model R^2:"
summary(reduced_mod_transformed)$adj.r.squared
## [1] 0.5469441
print("Transformed Model Without Obs 523 R^2:")
## [1] "Transformed Model Without Obs 523 R^2:"
summary(reduced_mod_transformed_clean)$adj.r.squared
## [1] 0.5472749
# RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)
rmse_transformed <- rmse(abalone$Age, predict(reduced_mod_transformed))
rmse_transformed_clean <- rmse(abalone_clean$Age, predict(reduced_mod_transformed_clean))

print("Transformed Model RMSE:")
## [1] "Transformed Model RMSE:"
rmse_transformed
## [1] 2.194679
print("Transformed Model Without Obs 523 RMSE:")
## [1] "Transformed Model Without Obs 523 RMSE:"
rmse_transformed_clean
## [1] 2.193888

To evaluate the impact of the influential observation identified earlier, we refit the transformed model after removing observation 523 and compared its performance to the original transformed model. The model without this point showed a lower AIC (66156.01 vs. 66171.23), a slightly higher adjusted R² (0.5473 vs. 0.5469), and a marginally lower RMSE (2.1939 vs. 2.1947). Although the numerical improvements are modest, they consistently indicate a better‑fitting and more stable model. This suggests that observation 523 exerted disproportionate influence on the regression surface. Given its combination of high leverage and large residual, this point may represent an abalone with atypical or abnormal characteristics. Removing it improves the model’s generalization and yields a specification that better reflects the underlying population pattern.

         Weight + Weight2 + Shell_Weight + ShellWeight2,
  data = abalone_clean
)

Removing Insignificant Interactions

mod_interactions_reduced <- lm(
  Age ~ Sex +
    Length + Sex:Length +
    Height + Height2 + Sex:Height + Sex:Height2 +
    Shell_Weight + ShellWeight2 + Sex:Shell_Weight + Sex:ShellWeight2,
  data = abalone_clean
)
summary(mod_interactions_reduced)

After fitting the full interaction model, we evaluated each Sex × predictor interaction to determine which terms meaningfully contributed to explaining variation in Age. The interactions involving Weight and Weight² were removed because neither the main effects nor the interaction effects were statistically significant, and their inclusion added unnecessary complexity without improving model fit. In contrast, the interactions between Sex and Length, Sex and Height, Sex and Height², Sex and Shell Weight, and Sex and Shell Weight² were retained because they were strongly significant and indicated clear differences in how these morphological traits relate to Age across sex categories. Removing the weak Weight interactions produced a more parsimonious and interpretable model while preserving the key sex‑specific growth patterns supported by the data.

AIC(reduced_mod_transformed_clean, mod_interactions_reduced)
##                               df      AIC
## reduced_mod_transformed_clean 11 66156.01
## mod_interactions_reduced      19 66201.37
print("Transformed Clean Model R^2:")
## [1] "Transformed Clean Model R^2:"
summary(reduced_mod_transformed_clean)$adj.r.squared
## [1] 0.5472749
print("Reduced Interaction Model R^2:")
## [1] "Reduced Interaction Model R^2:"
summary(mod_interactions_reduced)$adj.r.squared
## [1] 0.5461455
rmse_clean <- rmse(abalone_clean$Age, predict(reduced_mod_transformed_clean))
rmse_interactions <- rmse(abalone_clean$Age, predict(mod_interactions_reduced))

print("Transformed Clean Model RMSE:")
## [1] "Transformed Clean Model RMSE:"
rmse_clean
## [1] 2.193888
print("Reduced Interaction Model RMSE:")
## [1] "Reduced Interaction Model RMSE:"
rmse_interactions
## [1] 2.196037

To determine whether adding Sex‑based interaction terms improved model performance, we compared the reduced transformed model to the reduced interaction model using AIC, adjusted R², and RMSE. The interaction model performed worse across all three metrics: its AIC increased from 66156.01 to 66201.37, its adjusted R² decreased slightly (0.5473 to 0.5461), and its RMSE increased from 2.1939 to 2.1960. These results indicate that introducing the interaction terms added complexity without improving explanatory power or predictive accuracy. Although several individual interactions were statistically significant, their combined contribution did not enhance overall model fit. Therefore, the transformed model without interactions remains the preferred specification, offering a more parsimonious and generalizable representation of the relationship between morphological traits and abalone age.

Comparing Full Interaction Model to Reduced Transformed Model Clean

# Compare the full interaction model to the transformed clean model

# AIC comparison
AIC(reduced_mod_transformed_clean, mod_interactions)
##                               df      AIC
## reduced_mod_transformed_clean 11 66156.01
## mod_interactions              25 65905.48
# Adjusted R²
print("Transformed Clean Model R^2:")

summary(reduced_mod_transformed_clean)$adj.r.squared
## [1] 0.5472749
print("Full Interaction Model R^2:")
## [1] "Full Interaction Model R^2:"
summary(mod_interactions)$adj.r.squared
## [1] 0.5551888
# RMSE comparison
rmse_clean <- rmse(abalone_clean$Age, predict(reduced_mod_transformed_clean))
rmse_interactions_full <- rmse(abalone_clean$Age, predict(mod_interactions))

print("Transformed Clean Model RMSE:")
## [1] "Transformed Clean Model RMSE:"
rmse_clean
## [1] 2.193888
print("Full Interaction Model RMSE:")
## [1] "Full Interaction Model RMSE:"
rmse_interactions_full
## [1] 2.173613

To evaluate whether Sex-based interactions meaningfully improved model performance, we compared the transformed model without interactions to the full interaction model that included Sex × Length, Sex × Height, Sex × Weight, and Sex × Shell Weight terms (including their polynomial components). The full interaction model showed a substantial improvement across all metrics: AIC decreased from 66156.01 to 65905.48, adjusted R² increased from 0.5473 to 0.5552, and RMSE decreased from 2.1939 to 2.1736. These results indicate that, although some individual interaction coefficients were not statistically significant on their own, the combined set of interactions provides a markedly better fit and enhances predictive accuracy. This suggests that the relationship between morphological traits and Age differs systematically across Sex categories, and that these differences are best captured when all interaction terms are retained.

Before finalizing the interaction model, we conducted an additional sensitivity analysis to evaluate the impact of the youngest abalones in the dataset (Age = 1). Earlier diagnostic plots indicated that several of the most extreme residuals originated from this age group, and only a small number of observations fell into this category. Because such limited representation makes it difficult to infer reliable growth patterns for one‑year‑old abalones—and because these individuals may exhibit atypical or underdeveloped morphological characteristics—we examined whether their inclusion introduced noise or instability into the model. By comparing model performance with and without the Age = 1 cases, we assessed whether excluding these observations would yield a more generalizable and biologically coherent model for the broader abalone population.

sum(abalone_clean$Age == 1)

)

## [1] "Full Interaction Model Without Age = 1 RMSE:"
rmse_no_age1
## [1] 2.172752

Removing the Age = 1 cases produced a model with a lower AIC (65876.05 vs. 65905.48), indicating a modest improvement in overall model fit despite the models having the same degrees of freedom. Adjusted R² decreased slightly (0.55519 to 0.55476), but the change is negligible, and RMSE improved marginally (2.1736 to 2.1728). Taken together, these results suggest that the Age = 1 observations were contributing a small amount of noise to the model—enough to slightly worsen AIC and predictive accuracy, but not enough to meaningfully change the explanatory power of the model. Given that Age = 1 abalones are rare in the dataset and may represent biologically atypical individuals with underdeveloped or irregular morphological features, their removal yields a slightly more stable and generalizable interaction model without altering the substantive conclusions.

After evaluating multiple candidate models, including the transformed model, reduced interaction models, and full interaction models, the strongest overall performance was achieved by the full interaction model fit on the cleaned dataset with observation 523 and all Age = 1 cases removed. This specification produced the lowest AIC (65876.05) and the lowest RMSE (2.1728), while maintaining a comparable adjusted R² to the other models. These improvements indicate that incorporating all Sex × morphological trait interactions substantially enhances model fit and predictive accuracy. Removing the small number of Age = 1 observations further stabilized the model by eliminating biologically atypical cases that contributed noise. Taken together, these results support selecting the full interaction model on the cleaned dataset as the final and most generalizable representation of the relationship between abalone morphology and age.

Final Model

# Fit the linear model in R
Final_MLR_Model <- lm(
  Age ~ Sex * (Length + Height + Height2 + Weight + Weight2 + 
               Shell_Weight + ShellWeight2),
  data = abalone_no_age1
)

# View the model summary (includes coefficients and p-values)
summary(Final_MLR_Model)

Running Final Model on Test Set

# Load Test Data
Test_Data <- read.csv("./competition.csv", header = TRUE)

# Rename Variables to Match Model
Test_Data <- Test_Data %>%
  rename(
    Viscera_Weight = `Viscera.Weight`,
    Shell_Weight   = `Shell.Weight`,
    Shucked_Weight = `Shucked.Weight`
  )

# Create Polynomial Terms (No Log Transforms Needed)
Test_Data <- Test_Data %>%
  mutate(
    Height2      = Height^2,
    Weight2      = Weight^2,
    ShellWeight2 = Shell_Weight^2
  )

# 1. Predict Age Using Final Interaction Model
Test_Data$Predicted_Age <- predict(Final_MLR_Model, newdata = Test_Data)

# 2. Select ID + Predictions
pred_output <- Test_Data[, c("id", "Predicted_Age")]
